title: Glyceria fluitans
wikitext:
{{Short description|Species of grass}} {{Speciesbox |image = Glyceria.fluitans.2.jpg |genus = Glyceria |species = fluitans |authority = ([[Carl Linnaeus|L.]]) [[R.Br.]] | status = LC | status_system = IUCN3.1 | status_ref = {{cite iucn |author=Lansdown, R.V.|date=2014 |title=''Glyceria fluitans'' |volume=2014 |article-number=e.T164299A42384780|doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2014-1.RLTS.T164299A42384780.en|access-date=15 November 2024}} }} '''''Glyceria fluitans''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|syns]] ''Festuca fluitans'', ''Poa fluitans'', ''Panicularia fluitans''), known as '''floating sweet-grass'''{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }} and '''water mannagrass''', is a species of [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[grass]] in the genus ''[[Glyceria]]'' native to [[Europe]], the [[Mediterranean region]] and [[Western Asia]] and occurring in wet areas such as ditches, riverbanks and ponds. It has a creeping rootstock, a thick stem which rises to one metre. The leaves are long, narrow and pale green, rough on both sides, often folded at the keel which lies on the surface of the water. The species [[epithet]] ''fluitans'' is [[Latin]] for "floating".Archibald William Smith {{google books|ahNMkgoNJ7IC|A Gardener's Handbook of Plant Names: Their Meanings and Origins|page=140}} == History == Before the 19th century, the grains were widely harvested in [[Central Europe]] and [[Sweden]], and traded as far as [[England]].{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Nesbitt |first1=Mark |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=47 |isbn=0-415-92746-3}} It was cooked and eaten as [[gruel]]. == Flood tolerance == When a shoot is submerged in floodwater there is a strong reduction of diffusion of gases which limits oxygen and carbon dioxide availability.{{cite journal |last1=Colmer |first1=Timothy D. |last2=Winkel |first2=Anders |last3=Pedersen |first3=Ole |title=A perspective on underwater photosynthesis in submerged terrestrial wetland plants. |journal=AoB Plants |date=2011 |volume=2011 |article-number=plr030 |doi=10.1093/aobpla/plr030|pmid=22476500 |pmc=3249690 }} To handle the poor gas exchange while submerged, ''Glyceria fluitans'' forms a gas film around the leaves.{{cite journal |last1=Konnerup |first1=Dennis |last2=Pedersen |first2=Ole |title=Flood tolerance of ''Glyceria fluitans'': the importance of cuticle hydrophobicity, permeability and leaf gas films for underwater gas exchange |journal=Annals of Botany |date=2017 |volume=120 |issue=4 |pages=521–528 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcx083|pmid=29059317 |pmc=5737359 }} The gas film allows an increase in the gas exchange since the diffusion of gas within the film is rapid.{{cite journal |last1=Verboven |first1=Pieter |last2=Pedersen |first2=Ole |last3=Tri Ho |first3=Quang |last4=Nicolai |first4=Bart M |last5=Colmer |first5=Timothy D |title=The mechanism of improved aeration due to gas films on leaves of submerged rice |journal=Plant, Cell & Environment |date=2014 |volume=37 |issue=10 |pages=2433–2452 |doi=10.1111/pce.12300|pmid=24548021 |s2cid=2699676 |url=https://lirias.kuleuven.be/handle/123456789/454006 |doi-access=free }} ''Glyceria fluitans'' has two kind of leaves: floating leaves and aerial leaves. Floating leaves form a gas film only on the [[adaxial]] side, instead aerial leaves form it on both sides. The formation of a gas film is caused from the [[Ultrahydrophobicity|superhydrophobicity]] of the leaves, which is provoked by the special structure of the leaves. Indeed, they have a plicate shape with ridges and grooves, on the microscale they have convex papillose [[Epidermis (botany)|epidermal cells]] forming papillae and three-dimensional epicuticular waxes. A gas film vanishes typically after 2–6 days of submergence because the leaves become hydrophilic.{{cite journal |last1=Winkel |first1=Anders |last2=Pedersen |first2=Ole |last3=Ella |first3=Evangelina |last4=Ismail |first4=Abdelbagi M |last5=Colmer |first5=Timothy D |title=Gas film retention and underwater photosynthesis during field submergence of four contrasting rice genotypes |journal=Journal of Experimental Botany |date=2014 |volume=65 |issue=12 |pages=3225–3233 |doi=10.1093/jxb/eru166|pmid=24759881 |pmc=4071835 }} Regarding the beneficial trait of the gas film development, it can be said that ''Glyceria fluitans'' through it enhances the gas exchange and therefore the photosynthesis under flood conditions, but it is seen as a short term strategie. ==Environmental conservation== ''Glyceria fluitans'' is a component of [[purple moor grass and rush pastures]], a type of Biodiversity Action Plan habitat in the UK. This habitat occurs on poorly drained neutral and acidic soils of the lowlands and upland fringe. It is found in the South West of England, especially in Devon. At the [[Great Fen]], researchers are running trials with ''Glyceria fluitans'' in order to assess its physical and financial viability as a crop in [[Paludiculture|wet farming systems]].{{Cite web|title=Water Works {{!}} The Great Fen|url=https://www.greatfen.org.uk/water-works|access-date=2021-11-10|website=www.greatfen.org.uk}} ''Glyceria fluitans'' was chosen because it has been consumed by humans for a long time and because of its tolerance to a wide range of growing conditions.{{Cite web|last=|first=|title=Wetland Crop Glyceria|url=https://fensforthefuture.org.uk/creating-the-future/wetland-crop-glyceria|access-date=2021-11-10|website=Fens for the Future}} This tolerance originates from the fact that ''Glyceria fluitans'' is to some extent self-sterile and therefore [[Outcrossing|outbreeding]], which allows for [[adaptation]].{{Cite journal|last=Borrill|first=Martin|date=1956|title=A biosystematic study of some ''Glyceria'' species in Britain.|journal=Watsonia|volume=3|pages=291–298}} == Farming techniques == The use and cultivation of ''Glyceria fluitans'' disappeared little by little during the 19th and 20th century due to its long gathering time and the disappearance of [[wetlands]].{{cite journal |last1 = Luczaj |first1 = L. J.| last2 = Dumanowski |first2 = J.|last3 = Koehler|first3 = P.|last4 = Mueller-Bieniek|first4 = A.|date = 2012|title = The Use and Economic Value of Manna grass (Glyceria) in Poland from the Middle Ages to the Twentieth Century|url = https://gateway.webofknowledge.com/gateway/Gateway.cgi?GWVersion=2&SrcAuth=DOISource&SrcApp=WOS&KeyAID=10.1007%2Fs10745-012-9513-4&DestApp=DOI&SrcAppSID=F37fmylfhL6Ny1Ipkfl&SrcJTitle=HUMAN+ECOLOGY&DestDOIRegistrantName=Springer-Verlag|journal= Human Ecology|volume = 40|issue = 5|pages = 721–733|doi = 10.1007/s10745-012-9513-4|s2cid = 153349412}} For these reasons, known farming techniques are old and not very applicable to today's production systems anymore. === Harvest and postharvest treatments === ''Glyceria fluitans'' is harvested in the second half of June or early July. The maturation and harvest time of ''Glyceria fluitans'' were interesting for farmers in the past centuries because it preceded the wheat and rye harvest by 1 month, a period of significant cereal shortage. The grains of ''Glyceria fluitans'' were harvested with a sieve at the morning dew. The sieves were described with long handles and only strong people could use them. After the harvest, grains were dried out and grinded in a [[mortar and pestle|mortar]] filled with straw at the bottom so that the shells could be removed. The reasons why ''Glyceria fluitans'' grains were harvested at the morning dew are the following: firstly, grains tend to stick better to the sieves when humid. Secondly, the grains of dry plants tend to fall more easily on the ground at the smallest movement causing yield loses. However, these harvest techniques are not suitable for today's agricultural production and new cultivars through genetic breeding should be developed.{{cite journal |last1 = Hozyasz|first1 = K. K.|date = 2020|title = From rediscovered "niche" to "mainstream" - Glyceria fluitans as a candidate grain for manufacturing premium food products|journal= Plants People Planet|volume = 2|issue = 2|pages = 104–106|doi = 10.1002/ppp3.10070|s2cid = 210312934|doi-access = free}} === Sowing === The sowing of ''Glyceria fluitans'' takes place in summer. The seeding density is 8 to 12 [[Pound (mass)|lbs]] per [[acre]]. == As a food == ''Glyceria fluitans'' grains were popular in Poland, Germany, Hungary and other European countries for their sweet taste and nutrient richness. In Poland, foods containing ''Glyceria fluitans'' were pointed out as specialities of the local cuisine. Originally, ''Glyceria fluitans'' was used to prepare dishes as sweet cakes, flatbreads, dumplings, with butter or boiled milk, broths and soups, with oriental spices, as well as in sausages as binding additive. Due to its healthy properties, between the 17th and 18th century, [[pharmacopoeias]] advised its consumption to people with debilitating diseases as well as malnourished young people.{{cite journal |last1=Drobnik |first1=J. |title=Polish manna grass in the 16th to 19th centuries: A botanical and medicinal approach (in Polish) |journal=Etnobiologia Polska |date=2015 |volume=5 |pages=67–87 |url=http://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?hl=en&volume=5&publication_year=2015&pages=67-87&journal=Etnobiologia+Polska&author=J.+Drobnik&title=Polish+manna+grass+in+the+16th+to+19th+centuries%3A+A+botanical+and+medicinal+approach}}{{cite book |last1=Jourdan |first1=A. J. |title=Pharmacopée Universelle, ou Conspectus des Pharmacopées |date=1840 |publisher=Paris, France: J.-B.Bailliére |url=http://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?hl=en&publication_year=1840&author=A.+J.+Jourdan&title=Pharmacopée+Universelle%2C+ou+Conspectus+des+Pharmacopées}}{{cite book |last1=Schumacher |first1=C. Johnson & Co. |url=http://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?hl=en&publication_year=1812&author=J.+Stokes&title=A+botanical+materia+medica+consisting+of+the+generic+and+specific+characters+of+the+plants+used+in+medicine+and+diet%2C+with+synonyms%2C+and+references+to+medical+authors}} === Nutrition === ==== Nutrient content ==== 100 g of ''Glyceria fluitans'' grains (endosperm, ca. 13.5% water content) contain about: 9.69% of protein, 0.43% of total fat, 75.06% of carbohydrate (starch and sugar), 0.21% of dietary fiber and 0.61% of ash. {{cite journal |last1=Hartwich |first1=C. |last2=Håkanson |first2=G. |title=Über ''Glyceria fluitans'', ein fast vergessenes einheimisches Getreide |journal= Zeitschrift für Untersuchung der Nahrungs- und Genußmittel|date=1905 |volume=10 |issue=8 |pages=473–478 |doi=10.1007/BF02297944 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1758303}} ==Gallery== Image:Glyceria spp Sturm38.jpg|''Glyceria fluitans'' ('''1''')
